approved: Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 2) Bill 2018

The government's housing affordability bills are inadequate, as they fail to address negative gearing and capital gains tax reform, which the IMF supports; the Treasurer also killed the promising build-to-rent sector. Labor will not oppose the bills but calls for genuine tax reform and a national housing supply measure.

The speaker argued that the government's housing affordability bills do not address the core problems of negative gearing and the 50% capital gains tax discount, which primarily benefit high-income earners and inflate house prices. Labor's alternative policies would restrict negative gearing to new properties only and reduce the capital gains tax discount to 25%, aiming to reduce competition for first home buyers and increase housing supply.

The speaker argued the government's housing affordability bill is insufficient, calling for action on negative gearing and capital gains tax, and cited declining home ownership rates—a 60-year low—and rising investor activity as evidence of the crisis.

The government's housing affordability package was condemned as ineffective "do-nothing" bills, failing the 195,000 people on social housing waiting lists and 288,000 who sought homelessness services in 2017. Negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions were identified as fuelling demand and benefiting the top 20% of earners, while the proposed superannuation withdrawal measure was said to push up prices.

The speaker argued in support of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 2) Bill 2018, which implements tighter capital gains tax rules for foreign residents, introduces a reconciliation fee for developers selling to foreign persons, and provides a 60% capital gains tax discount for investments in qualifying affordable rental housing.
